feedback.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

If $x(t)=5{t}^{2}-2$ and $y(t)=k+3{t}^{2}$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(5{t}^{2}-2)(k+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(15{t}^{4}+(5k-6){t}^{2}-2k)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(3{t}^{5}+\frac{(5k-6){t}^{3}}{3}-2kt){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3+\frac{(5k-6)}{3}-2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & =0 \\ 3+\frac{(5k-6)}{3}-2k & =0 \\ 9+(5k-6)-6k & =0 \\ 3-k & =0 \\ k & =3\end{aligned}
$$
